title: Blood tests and monitoring
intro: This page is about the blood tests and reviews that go with gender-affirming hormone therapy. It covers what is checked for each medicine, when the sample is taken, and what it usually aims for. It also explains how to read your results. It is background reading, not a prescription. Fertility, sexual function, PrEP and surgery are on the [Fertility, PrEP and surgery](#/related-care) page. The forms each medicine comes in and the dose ranges are on the [Medicines, doses and formulations](#/doses) page. If you are about to start hormones, the first steps, including the first blood tests, are on [Where to start with hormones](#/where-to-start).

body: Blood tests are not something you pass or fail. They tell your prescriber whether the dose is doing what you both want, and whether anything needs watching.

For estradiol-based therapy, Australia's 2026 standards of care recommend a trough oestradiol above about 250 pmol/L [1]. The trough is the lowest level, just before the next dose. There is no fixed upper limit [1]. For people who want full suppression, they recommend total testosterone below 2 nmol/L [1]. The 2019 position statement suggested 250–600 pmol/L [2].

For testosterone-based therapy, the usual target is a trough total testosterone of about 10–20 nmol/L [1]. This is for the long-acting injection, Testogel and cream [1]. Testavan and the short-acting injections are tested at a different time and read against different numbers. See the testosterone sections below [1]. Other guidance differs. The 2019 position statement and the 2020 Australian GP guides suggest 10–15 nmol/L [2][3][4]. Australia's 2026 standards of care, which this site follows, give about 10–20 [1]. Testosterone also thickens the blood, so haematocrit (the share of the blood that is red cells) is checked [2][3]. If it is 0.50 L/L (50%) or above, the dose or the time between doses is usually reviewed [2][3]. The product information for several testosterone injections now also warns about SGLT-2 inhibitors [5]. These are medicines for diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease, such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin. Taken with testosterone, they have been linked to too many red blood cells. So the blood count is checked more closely [5]. This warning is not yet in every product information [6]. So tell your prescriber if you take one, whatever form of testosterone you use [6].

Reviews cover more than levels. They also cover blood pressure, weight and smoking [2][7]. And they cover how you are going in yourself: your mood, energy and sleep, and whether the changes match what you hoped for [2][7].

Screening follows the organs you have, not your gender and not your hormones [2][7]. If you have a cervix, screening is still due every five years [8]. You can collect your own swab. Many people find this far easier than a speculum examination [8]. The same applies to breast or chest tissue [7]. It also applies to prostate tissue, which genital surgery does not remove [7].
list: Estradiol-based: oestradiol and total testosterone. Electrolytes (blood salts such as potassium) and kidney function if you take spironolactone. Liver function if you take cyproterone [2][3]
Testosterone-based: total testosterone, and a full blood count for haematocrit. Liver function and lipids (blood fats) as your prescriber decides [2][3]
Either therapy: blood pressure and weight at each review. Glucose or HbA1c (blood sugar tests) and lipids from time to time, especially if you have other risk factors [2][7]
Puberty blockers: bone health is checked. This is because blockers pause the bone strengthening that puberty normally brings [2][7]

Before starting: baseline blood tests, with a pregnancy test if a pregnancy is possible. A routine blood-clotting test is not needed [19]. You also talk about fertility, and about contraception if pregnancy is possible. Neither testosterone nor oestrogen is reliable contraception [2][7]
Sexual health: STI and blood-borne virus testing as relevant to you, the same as for anyone [7]

Timing: Australia's 2026 standards of care suggest a review every three to four months in the first year. After that, they suggest a yearly review once things are stable [1]. Other guidance: the 2019 position statement suggests every three months in the first year, then every six to twelve months [2]. After a change to oestrogen, levels are rechecked six to eight weeks later, not straight away [3]. After a change to the long-acting testosterone injection, the Equinox guide waits two more injections [3]
sections.note: Screening and monitoring are easy to lose track of when you move between services. Ask your GP to keep a written list of what is due and when. Ask for a copy for yourself.

body: Each medicine below has its own table. It shows the tests usually done before starting, in the first year, and after that. The tables are a guide to what to expect, not a schedule to follow on your own. Your prescriber sets the actual timing. It can change with your health, other medicines and how you are going [1][2].

In the first year, reviews are usually every three to four months [1]. The 2019 position statement says every three months [2]. Once things are stable, Australia's 2026 standards of care suggest a yearly review [1]. The position statement suggests every six to twelve months [2]. Each table shows the test, when it is done, what it usually aims for, and when to talk to your prescriber. Under each table, "For clinicians" gives more detail and the page numbers of the sources.
Every review, whatever the medicine, also covers blood pressure, weight, mood and how the changes are going for you [2][7].
sections.note: Each medicine has a blood test guide to print, under its heading. Bring it to your appointment. Ask your prescriber to mark which tests apply to you. To keep track of your own results, use the blood test record: [Blood test record](/guides/log-blood-tests.pdf)

Liver deaths have been reported at doses of 100 mg a day and above, mostly in men treated for prostate cancer [12]. Australian guidance for estradiol-based therapy gives 12.5 mg once a week up to 25 mg a day [19].

AusPATH lists bicalutamide as not first-line, because of liver and lung harms, including deaths [13]. The lung warning was added to the product information on 9 July 2026 {{SRC:PI-BIC}} and published in the TGA's August 2026 safety update [14].

sections.h: Getting the timing of the blood test right
body: When the sample is taken matters as much as what is measured. Most targets in the guidelines are trough levels [2][3]. A trough is the lowest point, just before the next dose is due [2][3].
A sample taken at the wrong time can look far too high or too low, even when nothing is wrong. This can lead to a dose change you did not need.

For Testogel or testosterone cream, your prescriber will usually want the sample in the morning, before you put on that day's dose [3][1]. For Testavan, it is taken 2 to 4 hours after you put it on [1]. For the long-acting injection, the test is booked just before the next injection is due, not soon after one. For the short-acting injections, the sample is usually taken halfway between injections [1]. Estradiol implants are usually tested every 3 months in the first year [10].
sections.note: Ask for the right timing to be written on your pathology form. Tell the collection centre when your last dose was. It takes ten seconds, and it saves repeat tests.

body: Lab reports mark results as high or low using the sex on your Medicare or lab record. On hormones, that range may not fit your body. In the first year your prescriber may ask the lab for both the male and the female ranges [1].
A single flagged result is a reason to talk with your prescriber, not to change a dose on your own.

Units: Australian labs report oestradiol in pmol/L, testosterone in nmol/L, and haematocrit as a fraction (0.50 L/L is the same as 50%). Some overseas guidelines and apps use pg/mL and ng/dL instead. For example, 250 pmol/L of oestradiol is about 68 pg/mL. And 10 to 20 nmol/L of testosterone is about 290 to 580 ng/dL. If a number looks very different from the ones on this page, check the unit first. To convert: oestradiol pg/mL × 3.671 = pmol/L, and testosterone ng/dL × 0.0347 = nmol/L.
sections.listh: Things that can make a result look wrong
list: A sample taken at a different time after the dose from the one your prescriber asked for [1]

Estradiol gel on the skin where the blood is taken. Ask for the sample from the arm you did not put gel on [1]. It is sensible to do the same with testosterone gel or cream, though the guidelines do not say so
High-dose biotin, found in some hair, skin and nail supplements. It can make some oestradiol tests read falsely high. Tell the collection centre if you take it [1]
Splitting the dose, or letting tablets dissolve under the tongue. This changes when the level peaks [1]

Haemoglobin and haematocrit: these are read against the range for your affirmed gender once hormones have had time to work. That is about 3 months on testosterone, and about 6 months on estradiol. Your prescriber will tell you which range fits your hormones. On testosterone, the male range is used [1]
Kidney function (eGFR) is worked out from your creatinine, age and recorded sex. So the change over time tells you more than one result [1]
Iron studies: the range for your affirmed gender is used, unless you are pregnant or have periods. Then the female range is used. Your prescriber will tell you which range fits your hormones [1]
